title: Claim Bucket Sorter
description: Twelve invented practice records. Each pairs a planned poster claim with a source type and a quoted passage. None of the numbers are real findings.

buckets.name: VERIFIED
buckets.definition: A specific number matches a specific paper, with a quoted passage. Use the exact number.

buckets.name: DIRECTIONAL
buckets.definition: The direction is well established but the number differs across studies. Use a range or the best-supported single study.

buckets.name: QUALITATIVE-ONLY
buckets.definition: The effect is supported but not reliably quantified. Use a word such as "lower", with no invented percentage.

buckets.name: REJECTED
buckets.definition: No credible source supports the claim. Remove it, or replace it with a verified claim on a related subject.

records.claim: Students who took a 10-minute walk before class answered 9% more reading questions correctly.
records.passage: Participants in the walking condition answered 9% more comprehension questions correctly than seated participants (n = 212).
records.hint: Does the passage state the claim's exact number, from one specific study?
records.rule: The exact number appears in a quoted passage from a specific peer-reviewed paper, so the claim is VERIFIED and the poster can print 9%.
records.pattern: Exact number from a specific paper

records.claim: Pooled across studies, acoustic panels cut reported distraction by 5%.
records.passage: Pooling 18 studies, we estimate that acoustic panels reduce self-reported distraction by 5 percent (95% CI 3 to 7 percent).
records.hint: Is this number the review's own pooled result, or one borrowed from a single study it reviewed?
records.rule: A meta-analysis is the origin of its own pooled estimate, so quoting that pooled number is VERIFIED. The error would be citing a review for a number from one of its primary studies.

records.claim: In the study schools, library visits rose by 14% after a reading-buddy program began.
records.passage: Library visits rose 14 percent in the program schools over the same term, compared with no change in the comparison schools.
records.hint: Do the number, the subject and the setting all match the quoted sentence?
records.rule: The number, the subject and the comparison all match a quoted sentence in a peer-reviewed article, so the claim is VERIFIED.
records.pattern: Exact number from a specific paper

records.claim: Greener schoolyards reduce playground injuries by 30%.
records.passage: Across the included studies, injury reductions ranged from 8 to 30 percent, and all but one study found some reduction.
records.hint: Do the studies agree on the size of the effect, or only on its direction?
records.rule: The studies agree on the direction but not the size, so the claim is DIRECTIONAL: print the range 8% to 30%, not the largest value.
records.pattern: Top of a range printed as the number

records.claim: Shorter lecture segments raise attention scores by 15%.
records.passage: Of the primary studies reviewed, Study C reported a 15 percent gain in attention; the other studies found smaller gains.
records.hint: Whose number is the 15%: the review's, or one study's inside it?
records.rule: A review is not the origin of a number. The 15% belongs to Study C and the other studies found smaller gains, so the claim is DIRECTIONAL: trace 15% to Study C or print a range.

records.claim: Quiet reading corners increase reading time by 20%.
records.passage: Reading time increased in all three schools, by 11, 17 and 24 percent respectively.
records.hint: Is there one number, or several numbers pointing the same way?
records.rule: All three schools improved, but by different amounts, so the claim is DIRECTIONAL: print 11% to 24% instead of a single 20%.

records.claim: A view of trees lowers student stress by 25%.
records.passage: Students with a view of trees reported significantly lower stress, although the scales used do not allow a percentage change to be calculated.
records.hint: Does the source support the effect with a number, or only in words?
records.rule: The effect is supported but not quantified, so the poster says "significantly lower stress" and prints no percentage. A missing number is a legitimate result.

records.claim: Standing desks improve on-task behavior by 10%.
records.passage: The evidence suggests a modest benefit for on-task behavior, but effect sizes were too inconsistent to pool.
records.hint: Did the review produce a number at all?
records.rule: The review supports a modest benefit but declined to pool a number, so use words such as "modest benefit" with no percentage: QUALITATIVE-ONLY.

records.claim: Wood-paneled classrooms feel calmer to students.
records.passage: In interviews, students described the wood-paneled rooms as calmer than the painted rooms.
records.hint: Can a claim with no number be VERIFIED under the bucket definitions?
records.rule: VERIFIED needs a specific number. Interview evidence supports the effect in words only, so keep the word "calmer": QUALITATIVE-ONLY.

records.claim: Blue-light lenses boost test scores by 23%.
records.passage: Studies show students score 23% higher with our FocusShield lenses!
records.hint: Can you trace this number to a primary paper?
records.rule: A marketing page with no primary paper cannot verify a number, and no other source supports it: REJECTED.

records.claim: Classroom plants raise grades by a full letter grade.
records.passage: Research has shown that plants can boost grades by a whole letter grade.
records.hint: Which research? Is a study named anywhere?
records.rule: A blog post that cites unnamed "research" has no traceable primary paper, so the claim is REJECTED.

records.claim: Brighter classroom lighting doubles reading speed.
records.passage: Reading speed did not differ between the two lighting conditions.
records.hint: Does the passage support the claim, or contradict it?
records.rule: A peer-reviewed source does not rescue a claim it contradicts. With no credible support, the claim is REJECTED: remove it or replace it with a verified claim.
